explanations.explanation: Philippi it is, friend. The text calls it a Roman colony and the leading city of that district of Macedonia (Acts 16:12). Paul and his team stay there several days. Big city, and a lot happens in it.

Ephesus isn't the stop in this passage. The team goes from Neapolis to the Roman colony of Philippi (Acts 16:12). I know, friend, travel names can blur together like cookies cooling on a rack with no labels. Philippi is the one to remember here.

Corinth isn't where they head from Neapolis. The text says they go to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that district of Macedonia (Acts 16:12). Paul and his team stay there several days. Keep Philippi on your map, friend, because the rest of the story happens there.

Close, but the text says something different. After sitting down, they spoke to the women who had gathered there (Acts 16:13). So the people they spoke to were women, not men. One word changes the whole picture, friend.

Right, friend. The text says they sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered there (Acts 16:13). It was a riverside meeting outside the city gate, at a place of prayer. And a woman in that very group is about to matter a lot.

Yes, friend. The text says, “The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.” (Acts 16:14) Paul does the speaking, but the opening is the Lord's doing. Lydia, the dealer in purple cloth, listens and responds.

Her household does show up in the story, but not here. They come in a verse later, when she and her household are baptized (Acts 16:15). The text says, “The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.” (Acts 16:14) So the opener is the Lord.

The other women are there, since Paul's team spoke to the women who had gathered (Acts 16:13). But the text doesn't give them this job. It says, “The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message.” (Acts 16:14) Lydia's heart was opened by the Lord.

Not quite, friend. Lydia urges them, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house.” And the text says, “…she persuaded us.” (Acts 16:15) So the team stays with her. When a host like that makes the offer, the answer is yes.

That's right. Lydia urges them, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house.” The writer adds, “And she persuaded us.” (Acts 16:15) The team ends up at her house, and the story comes back to it at the very end. Her door stays open.

explanations.answer: They serve the Most High God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. She shouts, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” (Acts 16:17) She follows Paul and the team while she says it. The text only tells us what she shouts, so I'll leave it there.

The text never has her say that. She shouts, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” (Acts 16:17) No Jerusalem in that line. It's a good thing to hold onto the exact words, baker.

explanations.answer: They speak for the Roman gods
explanations.explanation: Roman gods never come up in her shouting. She says, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” (Acts 16:17) I get the guess, since Philippi is a Roman colony (Acts 16:12). But the words she picks are Most High God, baker.
That's the one, friend. Paul says, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” (Acts 16:18) He doesn't command it in his own name. He goes straight to the name of Jesus Christ.

King David is a great name, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” (Acts 16:18) The command rests on Jesus Christ. Nobody else gets the credit, friend.

Father Abraham doesn't come up in this moment. Paul says, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” (Acts 16:18) That's the name he speaks. Easy to mix up when the names pile up, friend.

Yes, friend. The text says, “And the spirit left her at that very moment.” (Acts 16:18) No waiting around and no second try. Paul gives the command in the name of Jesus Christ, and it happens right then.
The text says the opposite, friend. “And the spirit left her at that very moment.” (Acts 16:18) There's no delay. Her owners then see that their hope of making money is gone (Acts 16:19).

Yes, friend. The owners “…seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace.” (Acts 16:19) Silas is Paul's traveling partner, and he gets dragged along too. They did this when they saw their hope of making money was gone.

explanations.answer: Beg them to bring the spirit back
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have them begging. When they see their hope of making money is gone, they seize Paul and Silas and drag them before the authorities (Acts 16:19). It's grabbing, not asking. Silas, Paul's traveling partner, gets pulled in with him.

explanations.answer: Pay them to leave the city
explanations.explanation: No payment in this story, friend. The text says they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace (Acts 16:19). Silas is Paul's traveling partner. This happened when the owners saw their hope of making money was gone.

Yes, friend. The owners say, “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil” (Acts 16:20) Then they add a charge about customs unlawful for Romans (Acts 16:21). Notice what charge they lead with.

explanations.answer: Stealing the girl from her masters
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't record that charge. What they say is, “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil” (Acts 16:20) The girl and the money don't come up in what they tell the magistrates. Stick to the words in the text, baker.

Taxes never come up, friend. The owners say, “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans to adopt or practice.” (Acts 16:20-21) That's the whole accusation in the text. No tax talk at all.

explanations.answer: Fastens their feet in stocks in the inner cell
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The jailer “…placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks.” (Acts 16:24) He got the order to guard them securely, and that's how he carries it out. It's a hard moment for Paul and Silas, so let's just say it plainly.

explanations.answer: Chains them up in the prison courtyard
explanations.explanation: The text says something different. The jailer placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks (Acts 16:24). So it's the inner cell, not a courtyard. The location matters, friend, because it shows how securely they were kept.

explanations.answer: Moves them to a prison outside the city
explanations.explanation: No move in the text, friend. They were thrown into prison, and the jailer placed them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks (Acts 16:23-24). They stay put right where they are. That sets up the midnight scene next.

explanations.answer: Praying and singing hymns to God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God…” (Acts 16:25) Silas is Paul's traveling partner. The two of them are in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks after a beating (Acts 16:23-24). That's not what I would be doing at midnight.

explanations.answer: Quietly planning a way to escape
explanations.explanation: The text never says they planned an escape. It says they were “…praying and singing hymns to God…” (Acts 16:25) Paul and Silas are in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks (Acts 16:24). Prayer and song, friend, not plotting.

No arguing in the text. Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them (Acts 16:25). So the prisoners were the audience. Quite a midnight concert, friend.
Right, friend. The text says, “…the other prisoners were listening to them.” (Acts 16:25) Paul and Silas weren't singing to nobody. Even in that prison, somebody was paying attention.

The text says the other prisoners were listening to them (Acts 16:25). So it's true, not false. Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and they had an audience. A captive one, friend, but still an audience.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “At once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose.” (Acts 16:26) So the chains don't stay fastened. They come loose, every single one.

That's right, friend. “At once all the doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose.” (Acts 16:26) It's everyone's chains, not just Paul's and Silas's. The earthquake shook the foundations of the prison, and the doors flew open too.

Yes, friend. Paul calls out, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” (Acts 16:28) The jailer had presumed the prisoners had escaped (Acts 16:27). This is a heavy moment, and I think Paul's words come right when they're needed.

Paul doesn't say that. He calls out, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” (Acts 16:28) The jailer had drawn his sword because he presumed the prisoners had escaped (Acts 16:27). It's a heavy moment, so let's keep the words exact.

The text doesn't say that. What Paul calls out is, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” (Acts 16:28) The doors had flown open (Acts 16:26), and the jailer presumed the prisoners had escaped (Acts 16:27). I think Paul's words answer what the jailer was afraid of.

explanations.answer: What must I do to be saved
explanations.explanation: That's the question, friend. “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30) He asks it after he rushes in and falls trembling before Paul and Silas. Not a small question, and it gets a direct answer.

explanations.answer: Who sent this earthquake on us
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't record that question. The jailer asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30) He falls trembling before Paul and Silas, then brings them out and asks that. Stick with the exact words, baker.

explanations.answer: How did your chains come loose
explanations.explanation: That's not what he asks in the text. After bringing them out, the jailer says, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30) He's asking about being saved, not about chains. And Paul and Silas answer him in the very next verse (Acts 16:31).
Yes, friend. They reply, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:31) It's a short answer to a big question. And the household is included in it.

Rejoicing does come, but later. The jailer and his household rejoice after they have come to believe in God (Acts 16:34). The answer Paul and Silas give is, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:31)

Rest isn't the word they use. Paul and Silas say, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:31) The word is believe, friend. That's the one that goes with the Lord Jesus.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “And without delay, he and all his household were baptized.” (Acts 16:33) So no waiting. This all happens at that hour of the night.

That's right. “At that hour of the night…” the jailer takes them and washes their wounds, and “…without delay, he and all his household were baptized.” (Acts 16:33) No waiting at all, friend. The whole household is included.

explanations.answer: They have come to believe in God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. “…he and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe in God.” (Acts 16:34) The jailer brought Paul and Silas into his home. He set a meal before them. I think that's a happy house, friend.

explanations.answer: The jailer has earned a reward
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The jailer and his household rejoiced “…that they had come to believe in God.” (Acts 16:34) That's the reason it gives. No reward in sight, friend.

No pardon in the text. The reason given is that the jailer and his household “…had come to believe in God.” (Acts 16:34) The magistrates don't send their order until daylight (Acts 16:35). So the rejoicing comes first, friend.

That's the word, friend. Paul says they were beaten publicly without a trial and thrown into prison, “…even though we are Roman citizens.” (Acts 16:37) That fact is what alarms the magistrates (Acts 16:38). One word, big change in the room.
Soldiers isn't the word, friend. Paul says, “…even though we are Roman citizens.” (Acts 16:37) That's the fact that alarms the magistrates (Acts 16:38). Citizens is the word to hold onto.

Officials is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word in the text. Paul says, “…even though we are Roman citizens.” (Acts 16:37) The magistrates are the officials in this scene, and they're alarmed when they hear it (Acts 16:38). Citizens is the answer.

explanations.answer: Come themselves and escort them out
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, “Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” (Acts 16:37) He won't accept being sent off secretly. And the magistrates do come themselves (Acts 16:39).

explanations.answer: Pay them back for the beating
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Paul says, “Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” (Acts 16:37) That's what he asks for. Payment never comes up, friend.

explanations.answer: Put the slave girl's owners on trial
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't ask for that. After asking if they want to send them away secretly, he says, “Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” (Acts 16:37) The request is about the magistrates themselves. It's good to keep the details straight, baker.

Yes, friend. The text says, “After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house to see the brothers and encourage them.” (Acts 16:40) Lydia's door was open to them before the trouble and after it. Then they left the city.

The text says it did happen, friend. “After Paul and Silas came out of the prison, they went to Lydia’s house to see the brothers and encourage them.” (Acts 16:40) They stopped at her house first and then left the city. It's a quiet ending after a loud night.
